question_text: Mention the key features of meiosis.

page_header: Cell Cycle and Cell Division · 4 marks

steps.label: Two divisions, one replication
lines: Meiosis is two sequential cycles of nuclear and
cell division, called meiosis I and meiosis II.
The DNA is replicated only once, in the S phase
before meiosis I. After replication each
chromosome carries two identical sister
chromatids.
steps.why: Two divisions after one replication is the single fact that makes the product haploid. Every other feature of meiosis follows from this arithmetic.
common_mistakes: Writing that DNA replicates again before meiosis II. It does not.
Writing that meiosis is a single division.
steps.memory_tip: Two divisions, one replication. That is why four cells end with half the chromosomes.
steps.margin_note: Open with this. It is the feature every other one depends on.

steps.label: Pairing and crossing over
lines: In prophase I the homologous chromosomes pair,
which is called synapsis, and each pair forms a
bivalent.
Crossing over takes place between non-sister
chromatids, and the points of exchange are seen
as chiasmata.
This exchange produces new combinations of
genes, which mitosis never does.
steps.why: Pairing and exchange are the features unique to meiosis; naming them is what separates this answer from a description of mitosis.
common_mistakes: Writing that crossing over occurs between sister chromatids.
Leaving out the word bivalent or the word chiasmata. Both are marked terms.
steps.memory_tip: Synapsis, bivalent, crossing over, chiasmata — four words, all in prophase I.
steps.margin_note: Three short lines. Use the four technical words.

steps.label: Reduction and meiosis II
lines: At anaphase I the homologous chromosomes
separate and move to opposite poles, so the
chromosome number is halved.
Meiosis II follows without any further DNA
replication, and at anaphase II the sister
chromatids separate.
steps.why: Meiosis I separates the partners and meiosis II separates the copies. Keeping those two events apart is what the examiner checks.
common_mistakes: Saying sister chromatids separate in anaphase I.
Saying the chromosome number is halved in meiosis II.
steps.memory_tip: Meiosis I separates partners, meiosis II separates copies.
steps.margin_note: Two lines. Say which anaphase does which.

steps.label: The result

lines.text: One diploid cell → four haploid cells.

lines: Meiosis makes the haploid gametes or spores, so
fertilisation restores the diploid number and the
chromosome number of the species stays the
same from one generation to the next. The
crossing over in prophase I also makes each of
the four cells genetically different.
steps.why: The last mark is for the outcome, not the mechanism: four haploid cells, a constant species chromosome number across generations, and variation.
common_mistakes: Writing that two cells are formed. Meiosis gives four.
Writing that the four cells are identical. Crossing over makes them different.
steps.memory_tip: One in, four out, each with half the chromosomes and a different combination of genes.
steps.margin_note: Finish with the boxed result line even if you are short of time.

insider_note: This is a list question, so write it as separate features with the technical words — bivalent, chiasmata, haploid — rather than as a running paragraph.
